subcategory: Texas blackland prairie native cool-season bunchgrass

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto bare, well-drained clay or clay-loam soil in full sun; this cool-season bunchgrass germinates with autumn rains and greens up through winter.

directions: Broadcast seed onto cleared, well-drained clay soil in fall and leave uncovered or barely raked in, since this is the dominant cool-season grass of the Texas blackland prairie and germinates readily with the first autumn rains. It forms a low, arching clump of fine blue-green foliage that stays green through winter, sends up seed stalks tipped with long, twisted, needle-like awns in late winter and early spring, and then goes dormant and tan through the heat of summer. Its deep taproot makes it extremely drought tolerant once established and valuable for stabilizing heavy clay soils, though the sharp awned seeds can work into animal fur and should be mowed off before they mature in a lawn-adjacent planting. Pair it with warm-season bunchgrasses like little bluestem so the prairie stays green across both halves of the year.

subcategory: Texas blackland prairie native warm-season bunchgrass

planting.note: Direct sow in spring after soil has warmed into heavy clay or clay-loam prairie soil in full sun; this warm-season bunchgrass is a characteristic lower-growing component of blackland and coastal prairie restorations.

directions: Direct sow into heavy, poorly drained blackland clay or coastal prairie clay-loam in full sun, since this bunchgrass is adapted to the same dense alkaline soils that limit many ornamental grasses. It forms a modest, upright clump of pale grayish-green foliage topped in late summer by open, airy flower panicles that bleach to a whitish tan, giving the plant its common name and contributing fine winter texture and seed for birds. It tolerates both prolonged drought and periodic standing water better than most grasses its size, making it a useful filler species between taller bluestems and indiangrass in a prairie restoration or large native meadow planting. Cut the prior year's growth back in late winter before new shoots emerge.

subcategory: Texas blackland and coastal prairie native warm-season bunchgrass

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into well-drained prairie soil in full sun; plains bristlegrass is a widespread Texas prairie and grassland bunchgrass valued for forage and wildlife seed.

directions: Direct sow into average to lean, well-drained prairie soil in full sun; plains bristlegrass forms a neat, upright clump of fine grayish-green blades and sends up slender, bristly spike-like seed heads from late spring through fall that resemble a smaller, softer foxtail. It is markedly drought tolerant once rooted and persists on thin clay and caliche soils where many taller bluestems struggle, while still providing palatable forage and seed heavily used by quail and other grassland birds. Use it as a mid-height filler in a mixed native prairie bed or restoration seeding rather than as a specimen planting, and leave the winter foliage standing for seed and cover before cutting it back in late winter.

common_name: Gulf Coast Evening Primrose (Longflower Evening Primrose)
subcategory: Gulf coastal prairie wetland native wildflower

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into consistently moist to wet soil in full sun to light shade; this tall biennial evening primrose colonizes the damp swales and ditches of Gulf Coast prairie better than any other Oenothera in the region.

directions: Direct sow in fall into heavy, consistently moist soil along a ditch bank, pond margin, or low wet spot in full sun to light shade, where this towering coastal prairie primrose spends its first year as a basal rosette before sending up a thick flowering stalk the following spring. Large, soft lemon-yellow flowers open in late afternoon and through the night along the upper stem from spring into summer, fading to a warm apricot-orange by the next morning and drawing in sphinx moths and other night-flying pollinators. Unlike the smaller, dry-ground evening primroses common in Texas, this species actually prefers wet feet and is well suited to a rain garden or the damp edge of a coastal prairie restoration. It self-sows readily where soil stays damp, so thin seedlings the following fall to keep the stand from crowding itself.

subcategory: Texas blackland and coastal prairie native hemiparasitic wildflower

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into lean, well-drained prairie soil already growing a stand of native grass, since trailing ratany is a root hemiparasite that taps into nearby grass roots and establishes best among an existing bunchgrass sod rather than on bare ground.

directions: Plant or sow into lean, well-drained prairie soil within reach of an established stand of little bluestem, buffalograss, or other native grass, since this low, wiry-stemmed wildflower taps into nearby grass roots as a hemiparasite and rarely thrives in isolation on bare ground. Its silvery, hairy leaves hug the ground in trailing mats only a few inches tall, studded from late spring through summer with small, unusually shaped magenta-and-gold flowers that give it a jewel-like presence among coarser prairie grasses. Once established among its grass hosts it needs no irrigation or fertilizer and tolerates the thin, rocky or sandy clay soils typical of blackland and coastal prairie remnants. Because nursery-grown plants establish slowly and unpredictably away from host grasses, it is best introduced by seed scattered directly into an existing native grass planting rather than transplanted as a potted specimen.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into lean, well-drained clay or clay-loam prairie soil in full sun; seedlings overwinter as a small rosette and bloom the following late spring into summer, as part of a blackland prairie wildflower mix.

directions: Direct sow in fall onto lean, well-drained clay or clay-loam prairie soil in full sun, where seedlings overwinter as an inconspicuous rosette before bolting into slender, wiry, upright stems the following spring. Small, bright yellow, five-petaled flowers open for a single morning along the branching stem tips from late spring into summer, shattering by afternoon and renewing daily over a long bloom season. As a short-lived species of undisturbed blackland prairie clay, it depends on open, lightly disturbed ground to self-sow and persist, so it fits best scattered through a prairie wildflower mix among bunchgrasses rather than grown alone in a tidy bed. Avoid rich, heavily amended soil and supplemental irrigation, both of which shorten its bloom season and reduce reseeding.
